extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what kinds of inventions constitute patentable subject-matter (art, machine, manufacture, improvements), and legal tests for novelty, sufficiency, combinations, and improvements. Explains when application of known things is unpatentable and when new modes/arrangements render a claim patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: No patent for mere analogous application of a known thing
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot have a patent for applying a well known thing which might be applied to fifty thousand different purposes, for applying it to an operation which is exactly analogous to what was done before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test is whether the application is only a new occasion of use (analogous) or whether the effect itself is new. Examples/anti-patterns: A surgeon seeing a mercer's scissors and merely applying them to cut skin would not justify a patent; applying scissors to cut a different substance in an exactly analogous way is not new. The palm-leaf curling example: using an old process known for hair to curl palm leaf for mattresses was held a mere double use and not patentable. Contrast: using gas to singe lace fibres was held a use not analogous to previous purposes and thus could be new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty test when principle or agent is well known
rubrics_metrics.description: When the principle is well known, or the application consists in the use of a known thing to produce a particular effect, the question is whether the effect itself is entirely new, or whether only the occasion upon which the particular effect is produced is new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the occasion only is new (i.e., analogous application), then not patentable. If the effect itself is new, or new contrivances/combinations/arrangements are used even with known agents, those contrivances may constitute a new principle and support a patent. Examples: producing a new manufacture or producing an old manufacture by new means is patentable; merely applying an old process to a new article in a directly analogous way is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent must claim new mode/process, not result alone
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent can be for an effect produced in a given manner, or by a peculiar operation; it cannot be a patent for a result merely or for an effect only (e.g., admeasurement of time or expansive operations of steam are not patentable per se).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an old machine in its unaltered state produces new effects, that alone does not support a patent — there must be a new mode, process, machinery, or specific manner of producing the effect. The patentee must show some new mode or means that produces the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory categories of patentable subject-matter: Art
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'art' means any new and useful art or improvement of an art; it embraces cases where application of a principle is the most important part of the invention and machinery or apparatus is incidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies where the invention is principally a process/method of applying a principle or a new application of processes to produce a new effect (even if materials/processes are old). Example: new manner of printing bank notes (combining copperplate and letter-press on both sides) was held an 'art' patentable as a new application producing a new security against counterfeiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory categories of patentable subject-matter: Machine
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine must be a particular construction of mechanism containing the improved method of producing an old effect or the method of producing a new effect; it is a function embodied in a particular mechanism with its mode of operation and general structure pointed out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes new combinations of machines and new organizations of mechanism for a single purpose. A machine patent may cover machinery entirely new in all its combinations, or mechanism whose principle or modus operandi is new. Example: a telescope combining convex and concave glasses. Claims construction determines whether the claim is to the combination only or to specific parts as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination patents protect the combination, not separate machines
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the thing patented is a new combination of machines (whether the constituent machines be new or old), the patent is for the combination only; making the separate machines separately is not an infringement unless the whole combination is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent is limited by its terms to a combination, the statute gives remedy only for violation of that combination. Where several distinct independent improvements are in the same machine, a patent may be taken for them in the aggregate and will protect each improvement. But a patent solely for a combination does not prevent others from making/use of the separate machines absent use of the claimed combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement-of-machine patents limited to the improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for an 'improvement' of a machine is the same as a patent for an improved machine, but the patent can only be for the improvement or new combination added, not for the whole old machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a mere addition produces the same effects in a better manner, the inventor cannot claim the whole machine — only the actual improvement. Determining whether an alleged improvement is real and material (versus mere change of form) is key; this often requires assessing boundaries between known prior art and new mode of operation. Examples: patent lever in a watch — inventor's right limited to his actual improvement. If a specified improvement is pirated, that can be infringement; jury decides triviality vs materiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of principle/principles of a machine focuses on modus operandi
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'principles' of a machine, with reference to the patent act, mean the peculiar structure or constituent parts and the mode of operation (modus operandi); principles of two machines may be the same even if form/proportions differ, or different despite external similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In difficult cases skilled persons may be asked whether the principles are the same or different. The inquiry is whether the same effects are produced by the same mode of operation or by substantially different combinations and manner of operation. Examples: raising water by lever vs screw/pulley/wedge are different principles even if apparatus superficially similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlapping patents and improvements in force
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent that includes subject-matter of a still-in-force patent may be valid if only the improvement is claimed in the specification; the new patent comes into force after the old one expires or may be used under license/purchase while the old exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In infringement actions on an alleged improvement of a former patent, the specification of the former patent should be read; validity and remedies depend on whether the later patent claims only the improvement. Practical remedies while old patent runs include obtaining license or purchasing apparatus. Authorities cited support this practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to read prior patent in infringement of improvement cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In an action for infringement of a patent professing to be an improvement on a former patent, the specification of that former patent must be read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not material whether a machine constructed according to the first patent would be useful or not; if a machine constructed according to the subsequent patent is useful and claims only the improvement, the fact of utility of the first-specification machine does not bar consideration. This is part of evaluating novelty/priority of the improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency standard for alleged improvements (Buller J dictum)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there be anything material and new that will be an improvement of the trade, that will be sufficient to support a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expresses the practical sufficiency test: a real and material improvement to trade (not trifling) suffices. Determinations of materiality/importance are fact questions for jury or factfinder. See citations where triviality or significance was debated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of 'manufacture' as subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Manufacture' denotes anything made by the hands of man: vendible articles, substances produced by art and industry, and in some constructions processes of making or modes of carrying on a manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best general definition given: any new combination of old materials constituting a new result or production in the form of a vendible article, not being machinery. It may include a new process producing a known substance in a cheaper or more expeditious manner or of better kind. Examples and judicial definitions cited (Hornblower v. Boulton; King v. Wheeler).
